Unit-Level Estimation with Battese-Harter-Fuller

Source: vignettes/unit-level-bhf.Rmd
unit-level-bhf.Rmd

Overview

Unlike area-level models that aggregate data prior to modeling, unit-level models operate directly on individual survey unit records (e.g., households, farms, or persons) while linking them to population auxiliary aggregates (e.g., census means or satellite imagery).

The fastsae package implements the nested error regression model of Battese, Harter, and Fuller (1988) via eblup_bhf(), providing fast estimation and parallel parametric bootstrap MSE. hb_unit() fits the same model as a hierarchical Bayes model with INLA (see the last section).

Model Formulation

For individual unit jj (j=1,…,ndj = 1, \dots, n_d) in small area dd (d=1,…,Dd = 1, \dots, D):

ydj=xdj⊤β+ud+edjy_{dj} = x_{dj}^\top \beta + u_d + e_{dj}

where: - ud∼i.i.d. N(0,σu2)u_d \sim \text{i.i.d. } N(0, \sigma_u^2) is the area-specific random effect. - edj∼i.i.d. N(0,σe2)e_{dj} \sim \text{i.i.d. } N(0, \sigma_e^2) is the unit-level error variance. - udu_d and edje_{dj} are mutually independent.

The small area population mean Y‾d\bar{Y}_d is estimated by:

Y‾̂dEBLUP=X‾d⊤β̂+γd(y‾d−x‾d⊤β̂)\hat{\bar{Y}}_d^{\text{EBLUP}} = \bar{X}_d^\top \hat{\beta} + \gamma_d (\bar{y}_d - \bar{x}_d^\top \hat{\beta})

where: - X‾d\bar{X}_d is the known population mean vector of auxiliary variables for domain dd. - y‾d\bar{y}_d and x‾d\bar{x}_d are the sample means for domain dd. - γd=σu2σu2+σe2/nd\gamma_d = \frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_e^2 / n_d} is the shrinkage ratio.

Step-by-Step Example

1. Data Preparation

We use the classic cornsoybean dataset, reporting corn crop hectares per segment in 12 Iowa counties:

library(fastsae)
data("cornsoybean")
data("cornsoybeanmeans")

# Align column names for population auxiliary means
df_pop <- cornsoybeanmeans
names(df_pop)[names(df_pop) == "MeanCornPixPerSeg"] <- "CornPix"
names(df_pop)[names(df_pop) == "MeanSoyBeansPixPerSeg"] <- "SoyBeansPix"
names(df_pop)[names(df_pop) == "CountyIndex"] <- "County"

head(cornsoybean)
#>   County CornHec SoyBeansHec CornPix SoyBeansPix
#> 1      1  165.76        8.09     374          55
#> 2      2   96.32      106.03     209         218
#> 3      3   76.08      103.60     253         250
#> 4      4  185.35        6.47     432          96
#> 5      4  116.43       63.82     367         178
#> 6      5  162.08       43.50     361         137
head(df_pop)
#>   County CountyName SampSegments PopnSegments CornPix SoyBeansPix
#> 1      1 CerroGordo            1          545  295.29      189.70
#> 2      2   Hamilton            1          566  300.40      196.65
#> 3      3      Worth            1          394  289.60      205.28
#> 4      4   Humboldt            2          424  290.74      220.22
#> 5      5   Franklin            3          564  318.21      188.06
#> 6      6 Pocahontas            3          570  257.17      247.13

2. Fit BHF Model with Bootstrap MSE

We fit the model using eblup_bhf(). The domain-level Mean Squared Error (MSE) is estimated by parametric bootstrap (mse_type = "bootstrap", the default; mse_type = "none" skips it):

fit_bhf <- eblup_bhf(
  formula = CornHec ~ CornPix + SoyBeansPix,
  unit_data = cornsoybean,
  Xpop = df_pop,
  domain_var = "County",
  popsize_var = "PopnSegments",
  method = "REML",
  mse_type = "bootstrap",
  B = 50,
  seed = 123,
  print_result = FALSE
)

summary(fit_bhf)
#> 
#> ── Summary of fastsae Fit ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Call :
#> eblup_bhf(formula = CornHec ~ CornPix + SoyBeansPix, unit_data = cornsoybean,
#> Xpop = df_pop, domain_var = "County", popsize_var = "PopnSegments", method =
#> "REML", B = 50, mse_type = "bootstrap", seed = 123, print_result = FALSE)

#>                  beta std.error    zvalue pvalue

#> CornPix      0.366335  0.064959  5.639511 0.0000
#> SoyBeansPix -0.030364  0.067576 -0.449327 0.6532
#> 
#> Goodness of Fit:
#> loglikelihood           AIC           BIC

3. Inspect Domain Estimates

The resulting df_eblup data frame contains the domain estimates along with sample size, MSE, and Relative Standard Error (RSE):

head(fit_bhf$df_eblup)
#>   domain    eblup samp_size      mse      rse
#> 1      1 122.5825         1 81.64650 7.371235
#> 2      2 123.5274         1 69.94383 6.770354
#> 3      3 113.0343         1 80.17283 7.921429
#> 4      4 114.9901         2 52.75789 6.316599
#> 5      5 137.2660         3 32.60240 4.159698
#> 6      6 108.9807         3 59.61422 7.084763

4. Visualizing Results with autoplot

For unit-level models, domain uncertainty and model comparisons can be displayed with autoplot():

# Plot MSE across counties
autoplot(fit_bhf, type = "mse")


# Plot EBLUP estimates with confidence intervals
autoplot(fit_bhf, type = "comparison")

Hierarchical Bayes with hb_unit()

hb_unit() fits the nested error model with INLA and returns posterior means, standard deviations and credible intervals of the county means. It needs the INLA package, which is not on CRAN (https://www.r-inla.org/download/); the chunks below are only run when INLA is installed. The arguments are those of eblup_bhf():

fit_hbu <- hb_unit(
  CornHec ~ CornPix + SoyBeansPix,
  unit_data = cornsoybean,
  Xpop = df_pop,
  domain_var = "County",
  popsize_var = "PopnSegments",
  print_result = FALSE
)

head(fit_hbu$df_hb[, c("domain", "samp_size", "hb", "sd", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")])
#>   domain samp_size       hb       sd  ci_lower ci_upper
#> 1      1         1 122.7313 8.804362 105.47477 139.9879
#> 2      2         1 123.6795 8.656224 106.71329 140.6457
#> 3      3         1 112.3751 9.453466  93.84635 130.9039
#> 4      4         2 114.8302 7.949844  99.24851 130.4119
#> 5      5         3 136.6722 8.598466 119.81918 153.5252
#> 6      6         3 108.7452 7.372621  94.29483 123.1955

County by county, the posterior means are close to the EBLUP:

data.frame(
  County = fit_bhf$df_eblup$domain,
  n = fit_bhf$df_eblup$samp_size,
  eblup = round(fit_bhf$df_eblup$eblup, 1),
  hb = round(fit_hbu$df_hb$hb, 1),
  rmse_eblup = round(sqrt(fit_bhf$df_eblup$mse), 1),
  sd_hb = round(fit_hbu$df_hb$sd, 1)
)
#>    County n eblup    hb rmse_eblup sd_hb
#> 1       1 1 122.6 122.7        9.0   8.8
#> 2       2 1 123.5 123.7        8.4   8.7
#> 3       3 1 113.0 112.4        9.0   9.5
#> 4       4 2 115.0 114.8        7.3   7.9
#> 5       5 3 137.3 136.7        5.7   8.6
#> 6       6 3 109.0 108.7        7.7   7.4
#> 7       7 3 116.5 116.5        7.0   6.9
#> 8       8 3 122.8 122.6        6.6   6.9
#> 9       9 4 111.6 111.1        6.2   6.9
#> 10     10 5 124.2 124.4        6.2   6.0
#> 11     11 5 112.5 113.3        5.0   7.3
#> 12     12 6 131.3 131.3        5.3   5.7

The two sets of estimates differ by about 1 hectare at most (under 1% of the county means). The bootstrap root MSE and the posterior SD are different quantities; here the SDs are larger in 10 of the 12 counties (by up to half in counties 5 and 11), and with B = 50 the bootstrap MSE is itself noisy.

The prior of σu\sigma_u is half-normal with the scale of the unit responses (see vignette("hb-priors")). With 12 counties the posterior of σu2\sigma_u^2 is still skewed: its exact posterior mean is about 100 and its median 68, against a REML estimate of 63, and INLA’s summary of it (random_effect_var, 115 on these data) is not accurate. Do not compare it with the REML estimate of eblup_bhf(). The county estimates in df_hb are reliable: hb_unit() fits in INLA’s "classic" mode, which on these data matches the exact posterior (computed by numerical integration over the two variances) within 0.06 posterior SD, with SDs within 2%.

MCMC with engine = jax_engine()

hb_unit(engine = jax_engine()) samples the same model with NumPyro’s NUTS sampler instead of INLA (it needs Python with ‘jax’ and ‘numpyro’; see setup_numpyro_env()), and summarises the county means from the MCMC draws:

fit_hbu_jax <- hb_unit(
  CornHec ~ CornPix + SoyBeansPix,
  unit_data = cornsoybean,
  Xpop = df_pop,
  domain_var = "County",
  popsize_var = "PopnSegments",
  engine = jax_engine(chains = 4, samples = 2000),
  print_result = FALSE
)
fit_hbu_jax$rhat_max

It uses the same priors as the INLA engine. On these data its county means were within 0.16 posterior SD of INLA’s and its SDs 0.98-1.06 times INLA’s (four chains of 2,000 draws, largest R-hat 1.002). The differences are Monte Carlo error: against the exact posterior the JAX means were within 0.14 SD.

Counties without a sample

A domain that is in Xpop but has no rows in unit_data is predicted from the regression and its population means, in both functions. For example, without the sample of county 1:

cs_without_1 <- cornsoybean[cornsoybean$County != 1, ]
fit_hbu1 <- hb_unit(
  CornHec ~ CornPix + SoyBeansPix,
  unit_data = cs_without_1,
  Xpop = df_pop,
  domain_var = "County",
  popsize_var = "PopnSegments",
  print_result = FALSE
)
fit_hbu1$unsampled_domains
#> [1] 1
fit_hbu1$df_hb[fit_hbu1$df_hb$domain == 1, c("domain", "samp_size", "hb", "sd")]
#>   domain samp_size       hb       sd
#> 1      1         0 119.4547 10.52653

The population means in Xpop must be complete: a missing mean is an error, since the prediction of that county would be wrong. hb_unit() also fits binomial and Poisson responses (family) and a spatial county effect (spatial = "bym2" or "besag" with a proximity matrix W). For binomial and Poisson responses the county means are predicted at the mean covariates, which is biased for a nonlinear link (by -8% and -16% in a simulation; see ?hb_unit), and the function warns about it.

References

  • Battese, G. E., Harter, R. M., & Fuller, W. A. (1988). An error-components model for prediction of county crop areas using survey and satellite data. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 83(401), 28–36.
  • Rao, J. N. K., & Molina, I. (2015). Small Area Estimation (2nd ed.). John Wiley & Sons.
  • Rue, H., Martino, S., & Chopin, N. (2009). Approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models by using integrated nested Laplace approximations. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 71(2), 319–392.
